intro: The Qur'an does not tell its own story in order. It does not open with Muhammad's birth or end with his death. To read it well, Muslims and scholars alike turn to the seerah, the traditional account of the Prophet's life, and to reports about when and why each verse came. This unit gives you that context. It covers Arabia around the year 600, the twelve years of preaching in Mecca, the ten years of building a community in Medina, and the tools scholars use to connect verses to events.

You will read the earliest surahs beside the story of the cave of Hira, the short Meccan surahs beside the boycott and the Night Journey, and the long Medinan surahs beside the agreement of Medina, the battles, the treaty and the return to Mecca. You will also learn what historians can confirm from coins, manuscripts and outside writings, and what rests on Muslim tradition alone, and how to keep the two clear.

By the end you will be able to place a surah in Mecca or Medina and say why it matters, explain what an occasion of revelation is and how it changes a reading, describe the events of 610 to 632 as Muslim tradition tells them, and read a hard verse, including verses on fighting, with its context and with the ways its readers have handled it.
bigQuestion: How does knowing when, where and why a verse was revealed change the way its readers understand it?

timeline.t: Muhammad is born in Mecca, according to Muslim tradition
The first revelation in the cave of Hira, as Muslims tell it (Qur'an 96:1–5)
Public preaching begins in Mecca; the leaders of Quraysh oppose the message
A group of Muslims finds shelter with the Christian king of Abyssinia
The Year of Sorrow: Khadijah and Abu Talib die
The hijra to Medina; year one of the Islamic calendar
The battle of Badr; the direction of prayer turns to Mecca
The siege of the Trench; the conflict with the Banu Qurayza
The treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which Surah 48 calls a victory
The return to Mecca and the clearing of the Kaaba
The Farewell Pilgrimage; Muhammad dies in Medina
The caliph Uthman has an official written Qur'an sent to the main cities

words.d: the traditional biography of Muhammad, also spelled sira; the earliest major one is by Ibn Ishaq (died c. 767)
the Meccan tribe that guarded the Kaaba and controlled the city's trade; Muhammad's tribe
the cube-shaped shrine in Mecca; Muslims believe Ibrahim and Ismail built it, and they face it in prayer
a message that Muslims believe God sent to Muhammad through the angel Jibril; the Qur'an is the collection of these messages
the oneness of God; the central theme of the Meccan surahs
the two groups of surahs, dated before and after the hijra of 622; about 86 Meccan and 28 Medinan
the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622; year one of the Islamic calendar (AH)
a community; in the Qur'an and the agreement of Medina, the community of believers and those joined to it
the place where a ten-year truce with Mecca was signed in 628; Surah 48 calls it a victory
'the occasions of revelation,' reports of the situations in which Qur'an verses were revealed
commentary that explains the Qur'an verse by verse; al-Tabari's (died 923) is among the most cited
the Qur'an's term for Jews and Christians, as peoples who received earlier scriptures

test.q: Around the year 600, what was the main source of Mecca's wealth?
choices: Hosting pilgrims and caravans at the Kaaba
test.why: Mecca had no river or farmland; its shrine, well and place on the trade road made it rich.

test.q: Which two empires bordered Arabia around 600?
test.why: The Byzantine and Sasanian empires fought a long war from 602 to 628; Surah 30 opens with a reference to it.

test.q: Who wrote the earliest major seerah?
test.why: Ibn Ishaq (died c. 767) wrote it; it survives mainly in Ibn Hisham's edition.

test.q: According to Muslim tradition, what were the first verses revealed?
test.why: Most scholars hold that 96:1–5, beginning 'Read,' came first in the cave of Hira c. 610.

test.q: Which theme is central to the Meccan surahs?
choices: The oneness of God and the coming judgment
test.why: Tawhid, judgment and justice for the weak are Meccan themes; law and community rules are Medinan.

test.q: Which surah did Jafar recite to the Christian king of Abyssinia, according to the sira?
test.why: Surah 19 tells of Maryam and the birth of Isa, a story a Christian king would recognize.

test.q: What can historians confirm about Muhammad from outside sources?
choices: The words spoken in the cave of Hira
The details of the Night Journey
That an Arab prophet lived and Arab armies conquered widely in the 630s
test.why: Non-Muslim writings, coins and early manuscripts confirm the broad outline, not the individual stories.

test.q: What event does the Islamic calendar count from?
test.why: Umar set year one at the hijra; dates are marked AH.

test.q: What did the agreement of Medina say about the Jewish clans it named?
choices: They formed a community alongside the believers and kept their religion
test.why: The document says the Jews have their religion and the Muslims theirs, and each helps the other against attack.

test.q: Which battle in 624 does the Qur'an name in 3:123?
test.why: Badr, the surprising Muslim victory, is named in 3:123.

test.q: How does this course describe the conflicts with the Jewish tribes of Medina?
choices: As political and military conflicts between specific tribes in one town
As events not in the sira
test.why: They are told factually as tribal conflicts in wartime; readers debate their meaning.

test.q: What happened when Muhammad entered Mecca in 630, according to the sira?
choices: The idols were cleared from the Kaaba and most of the city was pardoned
test.why: Tradition describes a nearly bloodless entry, the removal of idols and a general pardon.

test.q: What is an occasion of revelation?
choices: A report of the situation in which a verse was revealed
test.why: Asbab al-nuzul are reports about why or when a verse came; al-Wahidi collected them.

test.q: How do most Muslim scholars read 2:256, 'There is no compulsion in religion'?
choices: As a general principle that faith cannot be forced
As a verse only about Meccan children
test.why: Most apply the rule that general wording counts; the debate is about the verse's limits.

test.q: What is the method this unit teaches for reading a verse on fighting?
choices: Read the verses before and after it, ask its occasion, and see how scholars have read it
Compare it only with the Bible
test.why: Context, occasion and the tradition's own readers are the three tools the unit practices.

write.prompt: Does knowing the occasion of a verse widen or narrow its meaning? Choose one verse from this unit (2:256, 2:190, 9:5 or 80:1–2), give its reported occasion, cite two other passages that bear on it (for example 9:4 and 9:6, or 22:39–40), and explain how at least two readers, such as al-Tabari and a modern scholar, have read it.
tips: Cite each passage as surah:ayah and name the translation you use (Pickthall, 1930).
Attribute every reading: 'al-Tabari reads this as…', 'most modern scholars hold…', 'Muslims believe…'.
Say what the occasion report claims and where it comes from (al-Wahidi, Ibn Abbas, the sira).
Compare readings; do not decide which religion is right.
Use the unit's terms: asbab al-nuzul, naskh, Meccan and Medinan, People of the Book.
